narrative.h2: Reggaeton video lives where the dembow and the dance floor meet

sections.heading: What reggaeton looks like
sections.body: Reggaeton MVs combine club energy with neighborhood specificity. The dembow rhythm dictates the edit — three-and-a-half beats, hard cut, repeat. Locations alternate between rooftops, club interiors with magenta wash, and street scenes that reference San Juan, Medellín, or Miami specifically. Wardrobe is fashion-forward: designer streetwear, statement jewelry, sometimes full couture in unexpected settings. Dance is participatory rather than choreographed — people moving with the song, not performing for the camera.

sections.heading: Reference points that actually work
sections.body: J Balvin's 'Mi Gente', directed by Daniel Duran, built the visual scale that reggaeton now operates at. Bad Bunny's 'Yo Perreo Sola', directed by Stillz, flipped expectations of who fronts a reggaeton MV. Maluma's 'Hawai' brings the cinematic narrative arm. Daddy Yankee's 'Gasolina' remains the foundational text every newer video answers to. Karol G's 'TQG' with Shakira, Feid's 'Normal', and Anuel AA carry the current visual language, while Colin Tilley's crossover direction work for the genre stays the industry default. The constant: real locations, fashion as identity, choreography that reads as natural movement.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Time the edit explicitly to the dembow pattern: 'cuts every three-and-a-half beats throughout the chorus, hold the bridge for eight bars'. Specify two contrasting locations and rotate between them — 'rooftop at sunset and underground club at 2 AM' creates the day-and-night arc the genre rewards. Wardrobe shift between locations should be dramatic. Tunee handles the magenta-and-amber club palette well when you name both colors and the haze level.
